scenes.heading: Node.js
scenes.caption: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, usually to build servers and tools. It uses the same language, with different built-in libraries: files, processes, and network, instead of the document. A server process stays up and handles many requests. A script runs and exits. Know which one you are writing.

scenes.heading: Step by step: Node.js
scenes.caption: Create the server or the script. Read the request or the arguments. Do the work without blocking the process on a long calculation. Listen for errors. An unhandled rejection can take the process down.

scenes.heading: Variables
scenes.caption: Variables are names for values. Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment. Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable.

items: Variables are names for values
Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment
Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable

scenes.heading: Step by step: Variables
scenes.caption: Give each value a name that says what it is for. Read a name to get the current value. Assign a new value when the fact changes. Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

items: Give each value a name that says what it is for.
Read a name to get the current value.
Assign a new value when the fact changes.
Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

scenes.heading: validation
scenes.caption: Validation checks that input matches the rules before you use it: required fields, shapes, ranges, formats. The check belongs on the server even if the form also checks. Browsers are not the boundary. Anyone can send a request by hand.

items: Validation checks that input matches the rules before you use it: required fields, shapes, ranges, formats

scenes.heading: Step by step: validation
scenes.caption: Write the rules next to the boundary where data enters. Reject the whole request with a clear message if a rule fails. Do not “fix” bad input silently. The sender needs to know. Check types and ranges, not only that the field is present.

scenes.heading: The event loop
scenes.caption: The event loop is how JavaScript does one thing at a time and still feels concurrent. It runs your code, then it runs the callbacks that became ready, then it waits for the next event. A long calculation blocks clicks and paints, because they are waiting in the same queue. Waiting on a network does not block, because the callback runs later.

items: The event loop is how JavaScript does one thing at a time and still feels concurrent
It runs your code, then it runs the callbacks that became ready, then it waits for the next event
A long calculation blocks clicks and paints, because they are waiting in the same queue. Waiting on a network does not block, because the callback runs later

scenes.heading: Step by step: The event loop
scenes.caption: Your function runs to the end. Timers, network, and clicks queue callbacks. The loop takes the next callback when your function has returned. A tight loop with no await starves the queue.

scenes.heading: Recursion
scenes.caption: Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until it hits a base case that stops. It matches problems that contain smaller copies of themselves, such as folders inside folders, or a list you handle one item at a time.

items: Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until it hits a base case that stops
It matches problems that contain smaller copies of themselves, such as folders inside folders, or a list you handle one item at a time

scenes.heading: Step by step: Recursion
scenes.caption: Write the base case first. It must not call itself. Write the recursive case so the input gets strictly smaller. Trust the recursive call to return the answer for the smaller input. Combine that answer with the one item you kept.

items: Write the base case first. It must not call itself.
Write the recursive case so the input gets strictly smaller.
Trust the recursive call to return the answer for the smaller input.
Combine that answer with the one item you kept.

scenes.heading: Detail: Recursion
scenes.caption: If the input does not get smaller, the calls never end and the program runs out of stack space.

items: If the input does not get smaller, the calls never end and the program runs out of stack space.

scenes.heading: Detail: Recursion
scenes.caption: The base case is not optional. It is the whole reason the process stops.

items: The base case is not optional. It is the whole reason the process stops.

scenes.heading: XSS
scenes.caption: Cross-site scripting, XSS, is when someone else's text runs as JavaScript in your users' browsers. It usually arrives as a comment, a name, or a URL you printed into the page as HTML. The script then acts as the victim: it can read their page and send their data away.

scenes.heading: Step by step: XSS
scenes.caption: Treat all user text as data, not as HTML. Escape it when you insert it into HTML. Avoid innerHTML for user content. A framework that escapes by default is a help, until you bypass it on purpose.
